BotGuideDialog.descExample:
Search only inside this repository. Do not use open web search.
When asked about a feature, read README and docs/ first, then answer with file paths.
BotGuideDialog.discoveryCaption: Every bot conversation runs in a terminal titled bot:<handle>. That title is the whole addressing scheme.
BotGuideDialog.figBody: Find where the retry logic lives under src/payment
BotGuideDialog.handoffCaption: A mention at the START of the message routes it. The recipient sees who sent it.
BotGuideDialog.p2: Whatever you write in a bot’s description is delivered to its agent as standing instructions — on every turn, on work a teammate hands it, and on scheduled runs. This is where scope belongs:
BotGuideDialog.p2b: A routine bakes the role in when you create it, so editing the description later does not rewrite routines that already exist — change those on the Automations page.
BotGuideDialog.p4: The recipient does not see your conversation — only the text after the mention, with your bot named as the sender. So write it as a standalone request: say what you want, where to look, and what to send back.
BotGuideDialog.p4bad: What does not work: “아까 그거 분석해줘” — the other bot has no “아까”. Nor does a mention buried mid-sentence, or one addressed to a bot with no workspace, which has nowhere to run.
BotGuideDialog.p4chain: To make a coordinator delegate every time rather than doing the work itself, put the rule in its description: “분석은 반드시 @analyzer 에게, 리포트는 @리포터 에게 넘겨라. 직접 하지 마라.”
BotGuideDialog.promptGood:
@analyzer src/payment 아래에서 재시도 로직이 구현된 파일과 함수를 찾아줘.
찾으면 파일 경로와 함수명만 정리해서 @리포터 에게 넘겨줘.
BotGuideDialog.r1a: Click a bot (or the ⚙ on its row) for its own screen: routines, settings, and the message box.
BotGuideDialog.r1b: Double-click to switch the main area to that bot’s agent session. If it has none, one starts first.
BotGuideDialog.r1c: A dot on a bot means another bot messaged it while you were elsewhere.
BotGuideDialog.r3a: A bot discovers teammates on its own only inside its OWN project, and only ones that have a workspace. Your own @handle is not limited that way — it reaches any bot in the roster.
BotGuideDialog.r3b: The handle comes from the name: lowercase, spaces become hyphens, Hangul is kept. “릴리스 점검” → @릴리스-점검. Rename the bot and the handle follows.
BotGuideDialog.r3c: When you message a bot, Orca first starts every same-project teammate that has no session yet (up to 6), so the roster is real before the bot looks at it.
BotGuideDialog.r3d: The bot then finds teammates with orca terminal list and writes to one with orca terminal send. If one is somehow missing it can start it with orca terminal create --title "bot:<handle>" --background.
BotGuideDialog.r3e: A bot with no teammates in its project is told nothing about delegation — it will just do the work.
BotGuideDialog.r3f: Two different ids are involved and mixing them up is the one thing that breaks delegation: the TITLE (bot:<handle>) is how a teammate is found, while --terminal takes the opaque "handle" field of that row (term_…). If you see a bot say the handle seems to have changed, it used the wrong one.
BotGuideDialog.r4a: Only a mention at the very beginning routes. “@analyzer 이거 봐줘” goes to analyzer; “이건 @analyzer 한테 물어봐” stays with the bot you are talking to.
BotGuideDialog.r4b: An unknown handle is not sent — you get told instead, so a typo never disappears into a conversation.
BotGuideDialog.r4c: This is the reliable way to hand work over. A coordinator bot delegating on its own is a judgement it makes, not something Orca enforces.
BotGuideDialog.r5a: A bot is not always on. It runs when you message it or when a routine fires, and a restart can end its conversation — the sidebar log is for this session only.
BotGuideDialog.r5b: The full conversation lives in the bot’s own agent session. Use ↗ in the bot’s header to open it; the sidebar shows only what Orca routed plus the latest reply.
BotGuideDialog.r5c: Each teammate Orca starts is a real agent process against your quota. Six is the cap for one message.
BotGuideDialog.r5d: Scheduled runs can be turned off fleet-wide by your administrator. Existing routines stay listed but do not start.
BotGuideDialog.rosterCaption: Bots are grouped by project. ◐ means the bot is working; ⏳ means it finished its turn and is waiting on a teammate it handed work to.
BotGuideDialog.s2: 3. Role and description are instructions, not labels
BotGuideDialog.subtitle: A bot is a named agent bound to one project. It has a conversation you can talk to, routines that run on a schedule, and teammates it can hand work to.

bot-guide-chat-sections.1837c5ec: Orca stores the room log, so it survives a restart. It records who said what to the room — each bot’s full reasoning still lives in that bot’s own transcript.
bot-guide-chat-sections.21e8296c78: Why the split: giving every bot its own chat window meant three bots were three windows, none showing what the others were doing — and a hand-off that failed looked like a bot going quiet.

bot-guide-chat-sections.4b6af81d: Double-click a bot in the roster, or press ↗ in the bot’s header, and Orca opens that session in the chat view for you.

bot-guide-chat-sections.6680296971: The chat surface is a ROOM, not a per-bot window: one bubble thread over SEVERAL bots, built from what their sessions report back. Open it from Rooms at the top of the Bots lane.
bot-guide-chat-sections.6d8c1a3f: ⚠️ A bot in a remote (SSH) workspace keeps its transcript on the other host, so the chat view cannot read it. Use the terminal there.
bot-guide-chat-sections.6d8c1a40: An @handle anywhere in the sentence addresses that bot — in a room it does not have to come first. @everyone or @all is the whole room, and so is naming nobody.
bot-guide-chat-sections.7e9d2b40: The sidebar thread stays an index either way: what you sent, what another bot handed over, and the one latest reply.
bot-guide-chat-sections.7e9d2b41: A bot that @s another bot pulls it into the next round.
